questions: Is 60 degrees acute, right or obtuse? How do you know?
segments.say: Right, acute, obtuse — spot the size. Show the arm swinging: a right angle is exactly 90 degrees, smaller than that is acute, bigger is obtuse. Keep your student notes open at the angle definitions for this scene.

questions: Where does the centre dot of the protractor go?
Which scale do you read if the baseline sits on the zero line?
segments.say: Measuring with a protractor. Line the centre dot up with the vertex and the baseline with one arm, then read where the other arm crosses the scale. Stress: vertex first, baseline second, reading last.

questions: Two angles on a straight line are 65 degrees and one unknown - how do you find the unknown?
How many right angles make a full turn at a point?
segments.say: Angles on a straight line, angles at a point. Two angles sharing a straight line always add to 180 degrees, and a full spin around one point is 360 degrees. Now try the angle questions on the worksheet in pairs.

questions: A triangle has angles of 90 and 40 degrees - what is the third angle?
Why does the corner-tearing trick prove the total is always 180 degrees?
segments.say: Triangle angle sum, quadrilateral corners. Tear the three corners off a triangle and they fit exactly onto a straight line: 180 degrees. The four corners of a quadrilateral add to 360 degrees.

questions: Why does a longer-armed drawing of 45 degrees still measure 45 degrees?
What would you say to someone who judges an angle by its arm lengths?
segments.say: Misconception: longer arms, same angle. Land the point: the angle measures the turn between the arms, not the drawing. Finish by taking the exit ticket on your own - its first question revisits exactly this trap.
segments.watchFor: The angle with longer arms is bigger. Listen and look for it in pair talk and on the worksheet: any answer that the longer-armed angle is bigger shows the trap - send them back to scene s5 and to the correct turn: An angle measures the turn between the arms: same turn, same angle, whatever the arm lengths.
